script_data.title: The Glitch of Criticism: Why Bad Outweighs Good
script_data.description: Ever received a wave of praise, only to dwell on a single negative comment? 🤔 Uncover the evolutionary brain glitch that makes bad feelings stick. Why does our mind over-index on negativity? Dive into this fascinating psychological paradox! 👇
script_data.script:
Imagine this: You’ve poured weeks into a passion project, finally sharing it with the world. The initial feedback is overwhelmingly positive. Ten different people praise your work, highlighting its brilliance, creativity, and impact. You feel a surge of pride, a sense of accomplishment. Then, you see it – a single comment, starkly critical, dissecting a perceived flaw, suggesting you missed the mark entirely. 

Suddenly, the ten glowing endorsements vanish from your mental foreground. The warmth of appreciation cools, replaced by a gnawing unease. Your mind latches onto that one negative remark, replaying it, dissecting it, trying to understand it. The praise, once so potent, now feels hollow, unable to counter the sting of the lone detractor. Your mood sours, and the joy of your achievement is significantly diminished, all because of a solitary voice of dissent.

This isn't a failure of your logic; it's a fundamental operating principle of the human brain, known as **Negativity Bias**. Our brains are hardwired to give greater weight and attention to negative experiences, threats, and information than to positive ones. From an evolutionary perspective, this made perfect sense. Missing a positive opportunity might mean missing a meal, but overlooking a negative threat – a predator, a poisonous plant – could mean death. Our ancestors who were acutely attuned to dangers were the ones who survived and passed on their genes. This survival mechanism manifests today as an ingrained **cognitive bias**.

Negative stimuli register more strongly and quickly in our amygdala, the brain's emotional processing center, triggering a 'fight or flight' response, even when the 'threat' is just a critical comment. This also links to **loss aversion**, where the pain of losing something (like social approval) feels twice as intense as the pleasure of gaining an equivalent positive. So, while your rational mind knows ten positives outweigh one negative, your primal brain screams: 'Danger! Flaw! Fix this!' This makes negative memories more vivid and enduring, and negative feedback disproportionately impactful.

Why bad feelings linger?
